impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 permits broad method claims for treating headache with an anti-CGRP antagonist antibody genus, where the functional limitation of treating headache adds nothing beyond the antagonist limitation, potentially allowing overbroad patent scope.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method-of-treatment patent claims against Eli Lilly's enablement challenge. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding undermines the Supreme Court's enablement precedent from Amgen v. Sanofi by sustaining overly broad genus claims for method patents. The decision creates important precedent distinguishing enablement standards for method claims from composition claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders, particularly in the pharmaceutical and biotech sectors, benefit from broader protection for method-of-treatment claims, as the court declined to extend Amgen's rigorous enablement standard to method claims covering a genus of antibodies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitor companies and generic/biosimilar manufacturers face broader blocking patents on therapeutic methods, potentially increasing licensing costs and delaying market entry for competing treatments.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award in a software trade secret misappropriation case.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's override of the jury's breach of contract award, reinstating it, while affirming Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation of automotive configuration software. This case addresses critical questions about appropriate damages methodologies in trade secret litigation involving complex enterprise software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors and trade secret owners benefit from the court's broadened acceptance of damages models and the reinstatement of the jury's contract damages award, strengthening their ability to recover for misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal software after licensing third-party technology face heightened risk of substantial trade secret misappropriation liability and damages, particularly when the licensing relationship ends.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive patent license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' sufficient for the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to enforcement-only operations triggered an automatic termination clause.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling the licensee to sue in its own name without joining the university. The court also held that the licensee's pivot to patent enforcement did not constitute cessation of business operations triggering contract termination. This clarifies standing rules for exclusive licensees in patent enforcement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive patent licensees, including patent assertion entities, benefit from clearer standards confirming their right to enforce patents independently when licenses convey all substantial rights, without needing to join the patent owner.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a procedural defense based on challenging standing of exclusive licensees, and universities/research institutions may have less control over how their patents are enforced by licensees.

impacts.caseName: Cocona, Inc. v. VF Outdoor, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a moisture vapor transmission rate (MVTR) range are indefinite when the specification identifies multiple testing methods that can yield materially different results, and the claims do not specify which method to use.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the asserted claims of a waterproof breathable membrane patent are invalid as indefinite because the MVTR limitation could be measured by different standardized methods yielding different results, and the patent failed to inform a skilled artisan with reasonable certainty which method defined the claim scope. This decision reinforces that patents claiming performance ranges must adequately specify measurement methodology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in materials science and manufacturing can challenge patents with ambiguous performance metrics, particularly where multiple industry-standard test methods exist and produce divergent results.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders claiming functional performance parameters face increased invalidity risk if their specifications reference multiple measurement standards without clearly identifying which one defines the claimed range.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a split decision on patent eligibility in a case involving communication technology patents used in television broadcasting standards. The court vacated eligibility rulings for certain patent claims while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed the jury's infringement and willfulness findings, and upheld the damages award. This decision provides important guidance on the Alice framework as applied to signal processing and communications standard patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical implementations in communications standards may maintain eligibility, and the affirmance of infringement and damages findings supports enforcement of standard-essential patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology implementers, including consumer electronics manufacturers, face continued exposure to infringement claims on standards-implemented technology, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about which claim formulations survive § 101 scrutiny.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in finding patent claims indefinite, and whether claims directed to a communications apparatus with a coupler matching impedance to air satisfy the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds. The court held that the patent's claims, while sufficiently definite, were not enabled because the specification did not provide sufficient guidance for a person of ordinary skill to practice the full scope of the claimed invention. This decision illustrates how enablement can serve as an independent ground for invalidity even when indefiniteness fails.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not reached below, providing multiple avenues for invalidating overly broad patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that even if indefiniteness challenges fail, courts may independently invalidate claims on enablement grounds, requiring specifications to fully support the breadth of the claims.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning when denying motions for Rule 11 sanctions and attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 in a case where asserted patent claims were found invalid under § 101 and related patent applications had been rejected on the same grounds.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the denial of sanctions and fee-shifting motions, holding that the district court's order lacked sufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The court emphasized that where a patent holder asserts claims after related applications were rejected under § 101 and after Alice, the district court must adequately explain its reasoning for declining fees and sanctions. This decision raises the bar for district courts explaining fee decisions in potentially exceptional cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers who prevail on § 101 grounds have strengthened prospects for recovering fees and sanctions when patentees assert claims despite prior § 101 rejections of related applications.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and their counsel face increased risk of fee-shifting and sanctions when pursuing infringement claims on patents with related applications that were rejected under § 101.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has jurisdiction over a dispute concerning interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement's contingent payment clause tied to the outcome of an ex parte reexamination.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a contract interpretation dispute regarding whether asserted patent claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination, finding the question was one of state contract law rather than patent law. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This decision clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for settlement agreement disputes that reference patent proceedings but are fundamentally contractual in nature.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements benefit from clarity that contractual disputes over payment obligations will be resolved under state law in regional circuits, potentially yielding more predictable contract interpretation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties who structure patent settlements with contingent payments tied to PTO proceedings may face jurisdictional uncertainty and potentially inconsistent results across regional circuits on the interpretation of patent-related settlement terms.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salt satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) for pharmaceutical compound patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that Exelixis's Malate Salt Patents have adequate written description, upholding the validity of patents protecting the active ingredient in the cancer drug Cabometyx. The decision reinforces that pharmaceutical patents claiming crystalline salt forms can satisfy written description requirements based on specification examples and disclosed properties, supporting Exelixis's patent protection through 2030.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical innovators benefit from confirmation that patents claiming specific crystalline forms of drug compounds can satisfy written description requirements, supporting lifecycle management strategies for branded drugs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face continued patent barriers to market entry, as courts uphold written description for crystalline salt form patents even where the specification describes limited polymorphic forms.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the term 'internal diameter' in an oil and gas tool patent and whether the resulting infringement and validity findings should stand.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded a patent infringement judgment involving oil and gas wellbore tools, finding issues with the district court's claim construction of 'internal diameter' in a patent directed to float tools used in casing operations. The case involves significant technology used in horizontal and deviated well drilling, an important sector of the energy industry.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the oil and gas equipment sector may benefit from more precise claim construction on remand, potentially narrowing the scope of asserted patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the energy services industry face uncertainty as vacated infringement judgments require relitigating claim construction, increasing costs and delay in enforcing their patents.
